reason: Swollen nodes are a normal grass and herb trait.
The examples describe how perigynia are held (appressed, ascending, spreading). That is a position or orientation of the perigynium.
A length-to-width ratio is meaningful for a sepal, and the examples state one.
'Base oblique' describes the shape (asymmetry) of the leaf base. PATO oblique orientation means the whole part is tilted. A rule should map 'oblique' on a base to base asymmetry, not to this term.
A thin pedicel is ordinary. One example, 'thin axillary peduncle', is a peduncle, but the pair stands.
Moss peristome teeth are described as divided to a given depth. The examples fit.
Fruits, including perigynia and follicles, can be ascending.
The number of branches of an inflorescence axis is a count that floras give routinely.
The examples say 'rachis flexuous'. The bearer is the rachis, not the whole inflorescence. A rule would need to attach a rachis to the right part (inflorescence axis) first.
PATO 'quality' is far too generic. The examples are lists of alternatives ('entire or divided'), and each alternative should be mapped to its own specific quality.
Androphore length is a normal measurement.
Colleter counts per leaf base or petiole are standard in Rubiaceae floras.

'Base acute' and 'apex acute' are normally leaf or bract features. A spike can have an acute apex, but these examples look misassigned. A rule would need to check that the part named is the spike itself.
Leaflet blade shape (elliptic, ovate, oblong) is a standard trait.
Hyaline, membranous sheath margins and bands are common, and 'transparent' fits that sense.
Stipe colour such as straw-coloured is standard in ferns.
A cyme can be terminal, axillary or lateral, and these are positions.
A loose sheath is a normal grass trait.
Fruit surfaces can be sericeous.
Thickened leaf margins are a standard trait.
Linear lobes are a standard shape.
Perianth lobes have colours.
Gemmae are described by colour in bryophyte floras.
Drupe diameter is a standard measurement.
Perigynia are described as inflated around the achene.
Lobes can be orbicular or suborbicular. Some examples are of a margin rather than a lobe, but they are few.
A thickening of the disc is meaningful. The examples read as a thickened ridge or midrib, so a thickening is the correct reading.
Trichome width is meaningful, and 'length by width' dimensions are given.
Truncate bases and apices are standard.
'Flowers few' counts the flowers. It does not say that the flower has fewer parts of some type. Use a count of flowers on the inflorescence.
Sepals can be filiform.
Spikes can be oblong.
Sheaths can be hairy.
Obscure or inconspicuous veins are a standard trait.
Surface texture (papillose, tuberculate) of a lip or labellum is standard in orchid floras.
Pinnule shape and base shape are standard.
Lip parts can be curved or upcurved.
'Capsule inclined' fits a capsule that is tilted. It is a true orientation.
Bud scales have colours.
A pentagonal blade is a normal shape.
'Winged petiole' means the petiole is winged, not the whole leaf. A rule would need to move the quality to the petiole or rachis.
Leaflet surfaces can be sericeous.
A terminal panicle is a standard position.
'Bulbiferous' means bulbils are present, and the pair says so.
A short column is a standard trait.
Obtuse apices are standard.
A tripartite lip is standard in orchids.
Capsule surface texture (papillate, furrowed) is meaningful.
The generic 'quality' term is too vague. The examples are lists of alternatives and each should be mapped to its own specific quality.
Pappus awn and scale length is a standard measurement.
Clasping and amplexicaul stipules are standard.
A stout or thick column is a standard trait.
Teeth can be triangular or deltate.
Fruits and capsules can be hemispheric. Some examples are of a cup or hypanthium, but they are fruit parts.
Inconspicuous rhizomes occur in the descriptions. A rule should handle 'without conspicuous rhizomes' as a negation.
Fronds have colours.
Pendulous spurs and short shoots are meaningful, and 'drooping' is the matching sense.
Stems can be bristly.
Corona segments have colours.
A keeled seed margin or seed is a valid trait, and the examples fit. Some say 'carinate'.
